corrections.how: Run Home Assistant OS in a VM on the Mac mini (VirtualBox is the documented route; the roadmap already plans this VM for the kids' speaker). Add the Hue, Sonos and LG webOS integrations, then the 'Model Context Protocol Server' integration with 'Expose all LLM APIs' turned off. Expose to Assist only the lights, speakers and TV, and create the token under a Home Assistant user made for OpenClaw. In OpenClaw add mcp.servers.<name> with url http://<ha-host>:8123/api/mcp, transport 'streamable-http', the long-lived token in an Authorization header supplied through a secret reference (not a config literal), and toolFilter.include written after a live probe of the tool names. Allow the server only to the stateless 'home' agent from F076; the registry before_tool_call hook blocks it for every other agent, checks each call's target against an allowlist of names and areas, and enforces quiet hours.
caveats: Home Assistant's MCP option 'Expose all LLM APIs' is on by default and the token belongs to an administrator account by default; both need tightening before OpenClaw connects.
The MCP server does not support notifications or sampling, so Home Assistant cannot push a state change to Happy through MCP; events need a separate webhook (see HOM-06).
A HomeKit accessory can pair with only one controller, so the LG TV stays in Apple Home and joins Home Assistant through the webOS integration, not through HomeKit.

Home Assistant's macOS page documents VirtualBox (UTM only as a fallback for people used to virtual machines) and points anyone not comfortable with virtual machines to a dedicated board; the VM is one more service to patch, back up and bring back after every reboot and FileVault unlock, and until it is up every home tool fails.
Running both the direct CLIs and Home Assistant doubles the paths to the same lamp; pick one.
With only Hue, two Sonos and one TV today, the hub pays off mainly if presence (HOM-05), announcements (HOM-03) or the kids' speaker are also wanted.

Home Assistant's MCP server offers its Assist intents plus any scripts exposed to Assist, not arbitrary actions; anything beyond on/off, brightness, volume and state reads (announcements, TV notices) needs a script a parent writes and exposes.

Because those tools are generic intents, toolFilter.include narrows verbs, not device classes; the exposure list in Home Assistant and a before_tool_call check on each call's target are the real limits.

The long-lived token is a ten-year credential for Home Assistant's APIs as one user; the exposed-entity limit applies to the MCP tools, not to the token, so it must stay host-side and be rotated by hand.
State text returned by Home Assistant (now-playing titles, device names) is third-party text read by an agent that can actuate; allowlists and caps in code have to bound the result.
corrections.safety: The home agent keeps no memory, has no web tool and no outbound message tool, so it holds no private data and cannot send anything out; the only outside text it reads is device state. Only exposed entities are reachable through MCP; locks, garage, alarm, gate and cameras are never exposed in Home Assistant, and a fail-closed hook that inspects each call's target repeats that block on the OpenClaw side (HOM-12). The token is a wider credential than the MCP tools and is kept host-side only.

corrections.description: A guardrail to set before any family iPhone, personal or the spare one, is paired with the Gateway. The Gateway's default ceiling for an iOS node covers location, contact search, calendar events, reminders, latest photos, motion queries and notifications; nothing flows until the operator approves the node's command surface and the phone grants the matching iOS permissions, but no further Gateway setting is needed. Only camera capture, screen recording, writes and Health need an explicit allow. Separately, the iOS app is always an operator client as well as a node.
corrections.how: List everything a phone should not answer in gateway.nodes.commands.deny (deny always wins), and add to gateway.nodes.commands.allow only the single command a feature needs. Turn off gateway.nodes.pluginTools.enabled so a paired device cannot publish tools to agents. Pair with the narrowest setup code that still works: --limited drops only the admin scope and leaves write, approvals and read; --voice-node leaves read and talk. Review the node's declared command surface before approving it, and again after any app update that widens it. Grant the nodes tool only to the agent that needs it, and have the registry before_tool_call hook block any call whose node is not the one assigned to that agent. Pair only Tony's own phone or a spare that is locked to the app.
caveats: The default table is a ceiling, not a promise: a command works only if the phone app also declares it, but a later app update can start declaring more.
A phone paired with the default (full) setup code also becomes an admin client of the Gateway.
An operator client with write scope can invoke enabled node commands directly, not only agents.

A limited setup code still gives the phone an operator token with write, approvals and read scope: whoever holds that phone can read every person's sessions and message any agent from the app. The docs describe operator scopes as a guardrail inside one trusted operator domain, not separation between people.
The iOS app does not finish setup without both node and operator credentials, so a node-only phone is not an option.
Push-to-talk commands are allowed by default for any node that advertises talk, outside the platform table; deny them by name if voice is not wanted.
Background wake-ups for App Store builds go through OpenClaw's hosted push relay, an outside service the Gateway must be allowed to reach; without it the phone answers only while the app is open.
The phone reaches a loopback Gateway only through Tailscale Serve, so every paired phone is also a tailnet device.
corrections.safety: This is the control that keeps a paired phone from turning a memory-holding agent into a reader of contacts, photos and location. It is enforced by Gateway policy and a fail-closed hook, not by prompt. It does not address the other direction: the phone's own operator token, which can read sessions and logs across the Gateway. Under the roadmap's rule that the control plane is the operator's alone, only Tony's phone or a locked spare should run the app.
unverified: No documented per-agent setting was found that limits which node the nodes tool may target, so the hook pin is assumed to be necessary.
Whether camera or Health commands still work on a phone paired with the voice-node profile.
Whether the phone's operator token can be rotated to a narrower scope after pairing without breaking the app.

corrections.how: Start with the simplest thing that works on a spare tablet locked with Guided Access: the family's shared calendar app, or a Home Assistant dashboard if HOM-01 exists. The OpenClaw route is a second step: one persistent 'board' session on an agent with no tools beyond reading the home-store; a scheduled agent-turn automation bound to that session, with a scheduled tool policy that allows show_widget, replaces named native report widgets (metrics, table, text and link blocks) with pin set to true; the tablet opens the Control UI through Tailscale Serve at that session with the dashboard expanded. Do not give the tablet a token with plain read scope, because that scope reads every session and the logs. The documented way to confine a viewer to one session is the Gateway roles system (a role limited to session reads, other people's sessions hidden, explicit membership of the board session), which needs a verified identity such as Tailscale for operator clients and is a Gateway-wide change to test first.
caveats: show_widget is offered only to clients that declare inline widgets, or to a scheduled job bound to a persistent session and limited to pinned widgets; a parent cannot text Happy over iMessage and get a widget.
A Control UI on the wall is an operator client of the whole Gateway; unless its scope is read-only, anyone in the kitchen can chat with an agent from it.
A native report is capped at 24 blocks and 8 KB, with no scripts or images.

The macOS panel needs the OpenClaw Mac app (not installed), shows one panel at a time near the menu bar and is render-only.

The read scope covers status, logs and session reads for the whole Gateway, so a read-only wall tablet can open either parent's conversations unless roles hide them; Guided Access with touch disabled is then the only thing in the way.
Once roles are configured, operator clients that present only a device or bootstrap token are refused, so every existing client's sign-in has to be rechecked.
The board is refreshed by a model turn, so it costs tokens on every refresh and can misformat; the printed sheet (HOM-14) needs no model.
Gateway restarts in the weekly patch window, tablet reloads and tailnet key expiry each leave the screen stale or blank until an adult reopens the expanded view.
corrections.safety: The board agent has no web tool and no outbound tool; it only formats data already in the family store. The display is an operator client, so its access has to be confined by a role to the one board session; a token with general read scope is not acceptable in a kitchen. Content shown is limited to what the family would put on the fridge. Kids see it but do not use Happy through it.

corrections.how: Route A: an allowlisted Shortcut named 'TV off' in happy's account, run with the shortcuts command by the F078 plugin; happy's Apple Account must be a member of the Home. reason: The never-list record is correct and well sourced. One of its three blocks is weaker than stated: Home Assistant's MCP tools are generic intents, so a tool-name filter cannot exclude locks or covers, and the Home Assistant token itself is not limited to exposed entities. The hook has to inspect each call's target, and the token's storage is part of the guardrail.

source_checks.note: Opened. Per-entity Expose control; locks and garage doors named as the sensitive devices. Default exposure of new entities is not stated.
Opened. Exposed entities only; 'Expose all LLM APIs' on by default.
Opened. Supported types include lock, cover (garage door openers) and alarm control panel.

Opened the abstract. Confirms title, authors, calendar-invite, email and shared-document injection against a production assistant, control of home automation devices, 73% of threats rated High-Critical, and risk falling to Very Low-Medium after the vendor's mitigations.
Lines 41-68: block is terminal.

corrections.how: Three independent blocks that a model cannot talk its way past. In Home Assistant, locks, covers, alarm panels and cameras are left unexposed to assistants and the MCP option that exposes every LLM API is turned off; this is the main block. On the OpenClaw side, the Shortcut name allowlist (F078) leaves out anything touching those devices, and toolFilter.include trims the MCP tool list, though it cannot tell a lamp from a lock because Home Assistant's tools are generic intents. The registry before_tool_call hook therefore inspects each call's target and returns block for any entity, area or domain on the never list, failing closed. The Home Assistant token stays host-side under a secret reference and never enters a sandbox or a prompt.
caveats: Home Assistant's HomeKit Device integration supports locks, covers and alarm panels, so the capability appears the moment someone pairs one.
The 9 Oct review found a gate-opener Shortcut in Tony's own account; the allowlist must name gates as well.
Published research showed a poisoned calendar invite steering a production assistant into controlling home automation devices; the vendor's mitigations lowered but did not remove the risk.
A human approval prompt is not a substitute here: isolated scheduled runs cannot approve, and approval fatigue is real.

Home Assistant's access token is a general API credential for its user, valid for ten years; the exposure list limits the MCP tools, not the token, so where the token is stored is part of this guardrail.
Exposure is a per-entity switch an adult can flip in a few taps; the hook's own never list must not depend on it.

reason: Honest as experimental, but the pairing step as written leaves an unattended phone holding an operator token that can read sessions and message agents. It also needs Tailscale on the spare phone, a hook pin because the nodes tool has no per-agent node limit, and a plain statement that driveway pictures can show the kids and neighbours and go to the cloud vision model.

corrections.how: Install the OpenClaw iOS app on the spare iPhone under happy's Apple Account, put the phone on the tailnet, and pair it with the narrowest setup code that still allows camera commands (try --voice-node first, otherwise --limited). Add camera.snap to gateway.nodes.commands.allow and deny every other phone command, camera.clip included (HOM-08). Keep the app in the foreground with Guided Access, touch disabled, and the app's keep-awake setting. The adult's main agent requests a snapshot through the nodes tool and names the back camera explicitly, since the default is the front one; the registry hook pins that agent to this one node and this one command. The JPEG goes to the vision model and the answer is one line with the picture. No motion watching.

Tailscale on the spare iPhone (the Gateway is reachable only through Tailscale Serve)
registry hook pin for the nodes tool (no per-agent node limit was found in the docs)
caveats: Camera commands work only while the app is in the foreground; a backgrounded app returns NODE_BACKGROUND_UNAVAILABLE.
Through glass at night the picture is mostly reflection.
A phone kept awake on a charger all year is a maintenance item of its own.
Outward-facing only; an always-available camera inside rooms where the kids are is not appropriate.
A low-cost network camera with camsnap (F079) is sturdier and can watch for motion; camsnap can also read a local webcam on the Mac.

An unattended phone running the app is an operator client: with a limited code it can read sessions and message agents, so Guided Access with touch off and a passcode is a security control here, not a convenience.
A driveway or front-step picture can include the kids, neighbours and passers-by, and it goes to the cloud vision model.
After a restart, an iOS update or an ended Guided Access session the app is no longer in front, and every request fails until an adult walks over.
corrections.safety: Read-only capture, sent only to the requesting parent. The image passes through the cloud vision model and may show children or neighbours, so it needs the same decision as other attachments, taken by both parents. The node is restricted to this one command by Gateway policy and the agent to this one node by a fail-closed hook; clips, which record audio by default, are denied. The phone's operator token is the weak point and is contained only by Guided Access and the narrowest setup profile that works.

Whether the spare iPhone could instead serve as a Continuity Camera webcam for camsnap under the happy account.
